questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why the same emissions convert two ways
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the same emissions convert to two reported quantities
questions.stem: A translator's note for the emissions chapter asks why one tonne is quoted two ways.

options.text: One is a mass of the gas itself, the other a mass of carbon equivalent, so the figures differ by a factor
One is measured at the source and the other at the vent, so the two figures differ by site
options.misconception: confuses the measurement point with the reporting unit

options.text: One covers the current year and the other the whole plant life, so the two figures differ by period
options.misconception: confuses the accounting period with the reporting unit

options.text: One is a verified figure and the other an estimate, so the two figures differ by confidence
options.misconception: confuses data quality with the reporting unit

questions.explanation: A mass of the gas and a mass of carbon equivalent differ by a fixed factor of 44 to 12 for carbon dioxide. Quoting the same tonne for both without that factor misleads every reader of the chapter.
questions.hint: Ask which quantity is being counted.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a price changes and what it leaves open
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish what a carbon price changes from what it leaves open
questions.stem: A glossary entry asks what a carbon price actually changes: one factory can cut emissions cheaply while another cannot, and both pay the same price per tonne.

options.text: It sets the total emissions allowed, so the factory that cuts least will be made to cut most
options.misconception: confuses a price instrument with a quantity cap

options.text: It changes the cost of emitting, so the cheap cutter gains the larger incentive to act first
It decides which technology every factory must adopt, so the cheapest option spreads to the sector
options.misconception: believes a price prescribes a technology

options.text: It pays factories for the emissions they avoid, so every factory earns the same for the same cut
options.misconception: confuses a price with a payment for abatement

questions.explanation: A price changes the relative cost of emitting rather than fixing an allowance, so plants with cheap abatement act first. Fixing a quantity is the job of a cap and allowance scheme.
questions.hint: Ask whether the instrument fixes a price or a quantity.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What free permit allocation transfers
questions.learningObjective: Explain what free permit allocation transfers
questions.stem: A translator's note asks how to render the word free in a permit glossary.

answer.exemplar: Set up a simplified market in which a fixed number of permits is issued for a sector and each firm receives its share for nothing at the start of the year, then lets them trade at a price. Track the money paid in trades, the value of the free permits at the market price and the effect on final emissions. The exercise should show that the free share is a transfer of the right to emit, whose value falls on the holder and rises on the public unless the allocation is auctioned.

questions.explanation: Giving permits away transfers their market value from the public to the recipient, while trading redistributes it among firms. Comparing free allocation with auctioning makes the transfer visible.
questions.hint: Follow the money attached to the permits.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Which variable each instrument fixes
questions.learningObjective: Identify the variable each policy instrument fixes
questions.stem: A translator's note for the policy section asks which knob each instrument turns.

answer.exemplar: A carbon tax fixes the price of emitting and lets the quantity of emissions float, so firms respond through abatement choices. A cap fixes the total quantity of emissions and lets the allowance price float, so firms respond by trading permits until the marginal cost of abatement is equal across the sector. A performance standard fixes an output or technology requirement for each unit and leaves both price and sector total to follow. The choice therefore determines whether the certainty sits in the price or in the quantity.

questions.explanation: A tax pins the price, a cap pins the quantity, and a standard pins an outcome per unit of activity. Once the pinned variable is known, the other follows from how firms respond to it.
questions.hint: Identify the variable each scheme holds constant.

questions.stem: A translator's note asks for the total charge paid by a sector: emissions are 1500000 tonnes a year, a fixed charge of 80 dollars per tonne applies, and firms cut 25 percent of emissions before paying.
questions.explanation: Firms cut 25 percent, leaving 1125000 tonnes to pay for, and at 80 dollars per tonne the total charge is 90000000 dollars. The charge is collected on what is still emitted, not on the original total.

questions.topic: The stage of an assessment that decides the project
questions.learningObjective: Identify the stage of an assessment that decides the project
questions.stem: A translator's note for the permitting chapter asks which stage decides the fate of a plant: screening, detailed assessment, consultation, or the permit decision itself.

options.misconception: treats an early filter as the decision itself

options.text: The consultation round, because the public response determines whether the permit is granted
options.misconception: assumes consultation alone can grant or refuse consent

options.text: The detailed assessment, because it holds the technical findings the decision later cites
options.misconception: mistakes evidence for the decision that uses it

options.text: The permit decision, because only it can grant or refuse the project and set its conditions

questions.explanation: Screening, assessment and consultation all feed into the decision, but only the decision grants or refuses consent and sets binding conditions. Treating an earlier stage as decisive confuses informing with deciding.

questions.topic: Why seven separate assessments answer seven questions
questions.learningObjective: Explain why separate assessments answer separate questions
questions.stem: A translator's note lists seven separate reviews and asks why they are not merged.

options.text: Each review covers a different time period, so merging them would produce an unmanageable document
options.misconception: attributes the separation to document length

options.text: Each review is run by a different ministry, so merging them would create a conflict of authority
options.misconception: reduces the separation to who holds the pen

options.text: Each review is required by a separate treaty, so merging them would breach international rules
options.misconception: assumes every separate review is treaty driven

options.text: Each review answers a different question, so merging them would lose the specific findings

questions.explanation: The reviews differ by the question they ask, such as ecology, heritage, noise and carbon, and each produces findings meaningful only against that question. Merging them into one verdict would bury the answers.

questions.topic: Two indicators and two denominators
questions.learningObjective: Match each emissions indicator to its denominator
questions.stem: A translator's note for the statistics annexe gives two indicators: emissions per unit of output, and emissions per capita. Which pair of denominators matches them?

options.text: Per unit of output divides by production, and per capita divides by population, so the two read differently
options.misconception: swaps the two denominators around

options.text: Per unit of output divides by population, and per capita divides by production, so the two read differently
Both indicators divide by production, because output is the only denominator a sector can influence
options.misconception: assumes both indicators share one denominator

options.text: Both indicators divide by population, because population is the only fair denominator between nations
options.misconception: assumes population is the only defensible base

questions.explanation: Per unit of output divides by production while per capita divides by population, and the two can move in opposite directions when output and population change at different rates. Swapping them inverts the conclusion.
questions.hint: Match each indicator to what it divides by.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why the same emissions convert two ways
questions.learningObjective: Demonstrate the two conversion bases on one inventory
questions.stem: A translator's note asks for a worked comparison of the two conversion bases.

answer.exemplar: Take one emission inventory with a stated gas mix, for example carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide, and convert it twice: first into the mass of each gas, then into carbon dioxide equivalent using the published warming potentials for the chosen assessment year. Ask learners to compute both versions by hand for one year of the inventory, then to check the totals against a conversion tool. The exercise should make clear that the equivalence factor depends on the chosen assessment year and on the gas being converted, so the same inventory yields different totals under different choices.

questions.explanation: Converting the same inventory two ways exposes the factor separating gas mass from carbon equivalent. Naming the assessment year shows the factor is a choice, not a constant of nature.
questions.hint: Convert the same inventory twice.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a price changes and what it leaves open
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a carbon price changes and leaves open
questions.stem: A translator's note asks what a carbon price leaves for others to decide.

answer.exemplar: A carbon price changes the private cost of emitting, so firms with cheap abatement options act first and the rest can wait. It leaves open the total quantity of emissions, the distribution of the resulting burden across firms, and the level of ambition, since the price is set by policy and can be changed. It also leaves the split between taxes raised and transfers avoided, which depends on how the revenue is used. A cap does the reverse, fixing the quantity and letting the price move to clear the market.

questions.explanation: A price alters incentives and lets the quantity float, so the sector total and the distribution of burden stay open to behaviour and policy choices. A cap fixes the quantity instead and lets the price respond.
questions.hint: Ask what a price does not pin down.

questions.topic: What free permit allocation transfers
questions.learningObjective: Compute the value transferred by free permit allocation
questions.stem: A translator's note asks for the value transferred to firms when 200000 permits are given out free and the market price is 45 dollars per permit. Give the total transferred value in dollars.
questions.explanation: Free allocation transfers the market value of the permits from the public to the recipients, which here is 200000 times 45, or 9000000 dollars. Without a price, the transfer is invisible in the accounts.
questions.hint: Multiply the permits by the market price.

questions.stem: A translator's note asks how a tax and a cap behave differently in one worked case: a tax of 30 dollars per tonne against a cap that cuts sector emissions by 20 percent.

options.text: The tax fixes the quantity of emissions and leaves the price open, while the cap fixes the price instead
options.misconception: reverses which variable each instrument pins

options.text: Both fix the same variable, and they differ only in how the revenue is spent afterwards
options.misconception: believes the two instruments differ only in revenue use

options.text: The tax guarantees a fixed sector total, while the cap guarantees a fixed unit price for every permit
options.misconception: attributes a guarantee to each wrong variable

options.text: The tax fixes a price and leaves the quantity open, while the cap fixes the quantity and lets price move

questions.explanation: Step one identifies the variable each instrument pins down: the tax pins price, the cap pins quantity. Step two follows how firms respond and what happens to the allowance price, which is why a cap needs a market.
questions.hint: Name the variable each scheme holds constant.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A fixed compliance charge across a sector
questions.learningObjective: Explain where a uniform charge concentrates abatement
questions.stem: A translator's note asks what happens when one charge covers a whole sector.

options.text: It sends more abatement to the firms with the cheapest options, concentrating cuts where they are cheapest
It spreads abatement evenly, because one charge per tonne means every firm cuts the same percentage
options.misconception: assumes a uniform price forces uniform effort

options.text: It raises every firm's costs equally, so no firm gains an advantage over the others
options.misconception: believes a uniform price equalises outcomes

options.text: It fixes the sector total, because a uniform charge on all tonnes prevents the total from rising
options.misconception: confuses a price with a quantity cap

questions.explanation: A uniform charge makes an avoided tonne worth the same to everyone, so firms with cheaper abatement cut more. The sector total falls by less than an equal-effort rule would deliver.
questions.hint: Ask which firms have the cheapest options.

questions.topic: The stage of an assessment that decides the project
questions.learningObjective: Identify which stage set the outcome in a consent record
questions.stem: A translator's note records one project: screening flagged it, the detailed assessment found no significant effect, consultation drew 300 objections, and the permit was then granted with conditions. What was the deciding stage?

options.text: The screening check, because it established which rules the project would be tested against
options.misconception: treats a scoping step as the decision

options.text: The permit decision, because only that stage could grant consent and attach the binding conditions
The consultation round, because 300 objections outweighed the assessment finding in the balance of views
options.misconception: assumes objections alone decided the outcome

options.text: The detailed assessment, because its finding was the substantive basis for the later decision
options.misconception: mistakes the evidence for the decision

questions.explanation: Screening, assessment and consultation each supply evidence, but the outcome and the conditions were set when the permit decision was made. The assessment finding was an input to that decision.
questions.hint: Look for the stage that set the outcome.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why seven separate assessments answer seven questions
questions.learningObjective: Design a comparison of seven separate reviews
questions.stem: A translator's note asks how seven reviews could be compared with one another.

answer.exemplar: Take the seven review reports for one development and build a matrix with one row per review and one column per theme, such as water, habitat, heritage, noise, air, carbon and community impact, marking each cell with the finding, the evidence relied on and the mitigation offered. Ask learners to attempt a single composite score from the matrix, then to argue which reviews could and could not be averaged. The exercise should make visible that reviews differ in scope, evidence standards and legal status, so a single number would hide rather than summarise them.

questions.explanation: A matrix showing scope, evidence and status for each review makes clear that they are not interchangeable pieces of one score. Attempting a composite reveals exactly what would be hidden by producing one.
questions.hint: Tabulate the reviews by theme and status.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Two indicators and two denominators
questions.learningObjective: Explain why two indicators can tell opposite stories
questions.stem: A translator's note asks why one emissions figure can look better than another.

answer.exemplar: Per capita divides total emissions by population, so a country with a large population can look modest per person while emitting a great deal in total. Per unit of output divides by the value of goods produced, so an efficient industrial economy can look clean per unit while consuming more material overall. A country with fast population growth and improving efficiency may therefore fall on one measure and rise on the other. No single indicator settles the question, because each embeds a different judgement about what should be held constant.

questions.explanation: Each denominator holds one thing constant and lets another vary, so the indicators can move in opposite directions on one country. Choosing between them is choosing which factor should not explain the result.
questions.hint: Ask what each measure holds constant.

options.misconception: believes a price pins the quantity

options.text: The price change is irrelevant, because only a binding target can change the emissions outcome
options.misconception: dismisses price incentives entirely

The price change guarantees a fixed reduction, because every firm faces the same incentive to abate
options.misconception: assumes a uniform response across firms

questions.topic: What free permit allocation transfers
questions.learningObjective: Explain what free permit allocation transfers
questions.stem: A translator's note asks which statement describes giving permits to firms free of charge.

options.text: It creates new emissions capacity, so the total of permits issued rises when allocation is free
options.misconception: confuses allocation with the setting of the cap

options.text: It removes the need for a market, because firms that hold permits need never trade them
options.misconception: believes free allocation ends trading

options.text: It guarantees lower emissions, because a firm given permits will have no reason to pollute
options.misconception: assumes a right to emit is never used

options.text: It transfers the value of the right to emit from the public to the firm holding the permit

questions.explanation: Allocation decides who holds the right to emit, and a free allocation hands that right over with its market value, so the public parts with an asset. It does not create permits or remove the market.
questions.hint: Ask who ends up holding the right to emit.

questions.topic: Which variable each instrument fixes
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a cap record with a rising allowance price
questions.stem: A translator's note records two years: in year one a cap of 1000 tonnes was met exactly with permit prices at 5 dollars, and in year two the same cap held while prices rose to 40. What does the pair show?

options.text: The cap fixed the quantity and the price cleared the market, so one fixed quantity can carry very different prices
The cap was tightened in year two, because a higher permit price can only follow a lower cap
options.misconception: infers a cap change from a price change

options.text: Both years were over-allocated, so the extra permits in year two pushed the price up by itself
options.misconception: invents a surplus of permits that the record does not show

options.text: The cap was loosened in year two, because the price rise shows that more permits were issued
options.misconception: reads a price rise as a cap change

questions.explanation: The permit quantity was unchanged and fully sold in both years, which is what a working cap looks like. The price moved because abatement costs and permit supply changed balance, not because the cap changed.
questions.hint: Ask which quantity stayed the same.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A fixed compliance charge across a sector
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of where a uniform charge has bite
questions.stem: A translator's note asks how to test where a uniform charge has bite.

answer.exemplar: Give a class of hypothetical firms different abatement cost curves, from cheap process changes to expensive capital rebuilds, and give each the same per-tonne charge. Ask them to choose the abatement each will undertake, then to plot the marginal abatement curve for the sector and mark the level at which the charge meets it. Repeat with a higher and a lower charge and compare how the total reduction responds. The exercise should show that the charge fixes a price signal while the firms with the cheapest options provide most of the reduction.

questions.explanation: Cost curves make clear which firms act first under a given charge, so the concentration of cuts becomes visible. Varying the charge shows how much the sector total responds.
questions.hint: Give firms different abatement costs.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The stage of an assessment that decides the project
questions.learningObjective: Explain which part of a consent process binds
questions.stem: A translator's note asks which part of the consent text carries legal force.

answer.exemplar: The decision stage is where the authority grants or refuses consent and states the conditions that must be met, so it is the only stage that creates an enforceable obligation on the applicant. The earlier stages, screening, assessment and consultation, generate evidence and views that the decision then weighs. Their findings are not binding on their own, and they cannot be relied on later if the decision departs from them. Translators should therefore avoid language suggesting that an assessment finding is a permit.

questions.explanation: Only the decision grants or refuses consent and sets enforceable conditions, while the earlier stages produce evidence the decision weighs. Their findings bind nobody until the decision adopts them.
questions.hint: Ask which text creates an obligation.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What free permit allocation transfers
questions.learningObjective: Compare free allocation with auctioning
questions.stem: A translator's note asks how to compare free allocation with auctioning.

answer.exemplar: Run the same sector twice with identical abatement cost curves and a fixed cap. In the first run, give firms their permits free and let them trade; in the second, auction the same permits and let the proceeds fund a support scheme for households facing higher energy prices. Compare the final permit price, the distribution of costs and the abatement achieved in each run, and then change the support scheme to see how much of the distribution difference is policy rather than market.

questions.explanation: Running the same sector twice isolates allocation as the only difference, so differences in distribution are attributable to it. Changing the revenue use then shows how much is policy rather than market.
questions.hint: Change only the allocation rule between runs.

questions.topic: Which variable each instrument fixes
questions.learningObjective: Explain which variable a tax, a cap and a standard each fix
questions.stem: A glossary entry for the policy annexe separates a tax from a cap from a standard.

answer.exemplar: A tax fixes the price of emitting and lets the quantity of emissions float, so firms respond by cutting wherever abatement is cheapest and the sector total falls out of that response. A cap fixes the total quantity and lets the allowance price float, so firms trade until the marginal cost of abatement is equal across the sector. A performance standard fixes a requirement per unit of output and leaves both price and total to follow from the firms' choices. The certainty therefore sits in a different place in each case, which is what a glossary entry should make plain.

questions.explanation: A tax pins price, a cap pins quantity and a standard pins a requirement per unit, so the free variable differs in every case. Once the pinned variable is known, the other follows from how firms respond.
questions.hint: Identify what each scheme holds constant.

questions.topic: The stage of an assessment that decides the project
questions.learningObjective: Read a consent record to find the deciding stage

The assessment effectively decided the matter, because the refusal simply followed its finding

options.misconception: invents a hidden third decision

options.misconception: denies the decision maker any judgement

answer.exemplar: Present the same inventory twice, first converted with the factor set used in an earlier reporting year and then with the set used for the current year, and ask learners to recompute the totals and to identify which gases account for the difference. questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a price changes and what it leaves open
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a carbon price changes and leaves open
questions.stem: A translator's note asks what a carbon price is and is not.

answer.exemplar: A carbon price makes emitting more expensive, which shifts effort towards abatement wherever it is cheapest and changes the returns to investment in cleaner equipment. It leaves the total quantity of emissions undetermined, since that depends on how many firms respond and how far they can go. It also leaves open how much of the burden falls on consumers through higher prices, how the revenue is used, and how the price compares in other countries. Translators should resist rendering a price as a quota or a target.

questions.explanation: A price shifts incentives and leaves quantity, incidence and revenue use open. Rendering it as a quota or a target would turn a flexible instrument into a fixed one in the target language.
questions.hint: Separate what is fixed from what is left open.

questions.hint: Divide the free permits by the total issued.

options.misconception: confuses a rate with a ceiling on the rate

questions.explanation: A flat rate sets one price for every tonne, so firms choose where to reduce, and those with the cheapest options reduce most. It is neither graduated, tradable nor capped as the others describe.

questions.learningObjective: Design a comparison of seven separate reviews
questions.stem: A translator's note asks how seven reviews could be judged.

answer.exemplar: Take the seven review reports for one development and build a matrix with one row per review and one column per theme, covering water, habitat, heritage, noise, air, carbon and community impact. Mark each cell with the finding, the evidence relied on and the mitigation offered. Ask learners to identify which reviews could be averaged and which could not, and to write the reasons into a shared protocol for future reporting. The exercise should end with a stated rule for combining findings without losing the difference between them.

questions.explanation: The matrix makes each review's question and evidence visible, so learners can see which findings may be combined and which may not. The protocol preserves the difference between the reviews rather than erasing it.

questions.topic: Two indicators and two denominators
questions.learningObjective: Explain why choosing an indicator is a policy judgement
questions.stem: A translator's note asks how to render the two statistical annexes.

answer.exemplar: Each indicator answers a different question and each is chosen by the question a reader wants answered. Per capita treats each person's share of emissions as the unit of fairness, so it makes a populous country look reasonable and a small wealthy one look careless. Per unit of output treats the goods produced as the unit of fairness, so it rewards efficiency and ignores the volume of consumption. Neither is neutral, because each embeds a decision about what should be held constant, and a translator who renders one as the other changes the argument of the document.

questions.explanation: Each indicator embeds a judgement about what to hold constant, so selecting one is a policy decision about fairness. Rendering them interchangeably changes the argument of the document.
questions.hint: Ask what each measure treats as fair.

questions.topic: A fixed compliance charge across a sector
questions.learningObjective: Design a test of where a uniform charge acts
questions.stem: A translator's note asks how to test a uniform charge.

answer.exemplar: Give a class of hypothetical firms different abatement cost curves, from cheap process changes to expensive capital rebuilds, and give each the same per-tonne charge. Ask them to choose the abatement each will undertake, then to plot the marginal abatement curve for the sector and mark the level at which the charge meets it. Repeat with a higher and a lower charge and compare how the total reduction responds. The exercise should end with a written note that the charge fixes a price signal while the firms with the cheapest options supply most of the reduction.

questions.explanation: Cost curves reveal which firms act first under a given charge, so the concentration of cuts becomes visible. Varying the charge shows how much the sector total responds.
questions.hint: Give firms different abatement costs.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The stage of an assessment that decides the project
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a consent decision does
questions.stem: A translator's note asks what a consent decision does.

answer.exemplar: A consent decision is the only stage that grants or refuses permission and states the conditions that must be met, so it is the only stage that creates an enforceable obligation on the applicant. Screening, technical assessment and consultation generate evidence and views that the decision then weighs, and they bind nobody until the decision adopts them. Monitoring comes after the decision and checks compliance with the conditions already set. A translator who renders an assessment finding or a monitoring report as a decision would misrepresent the legal position in the target language.

questions.explanation: Only the decision grants or refuses permission and creates obligations, while earlier stages produce evidence and monitoring checks what was already set. Confusing them misstates the legal position.
questions.hint: Ask which stage creates the obligation.

questions.topic: What free permit allocation transfers
questions.learningObjective: Compare free allocation with auctioning
questions.stem: A translator's note asks how free allocation compares with auctioning.

answer.exemplar: Run the same sector twice with identical abatement cost curves and a fixed cap. In the first run, give firms their permits free and let them trade; in the second, auction the same permits and let the proceeds fund support for households facing higher energy prices. Compare the final permit price, the distribution of costs and the abatement achieved in each run, then change the support scheme to see how much of the distribution difference is policy rather than market. The exercise should end with a written comparison of the two allocation routes.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Which variable each instrument fixes
questions.learningObjective: Explain why instrument choice decides where certainty sits
questions.stem: A translator's note asks how the choice of instrument is described.

answer.exemplar: Each instrument places the certainty in a different place. A tax guarantees the price of emitting and leaves the sector total to emerge from the choices of hundreds of firms, so it offers price certainty and quantity uncertainty. A cap guarantees the total and offers quantity certainty, with the allowance price moving to balance abatement across the sector. A standard guarantees a performance level for each unit and offers neither, leaving both price and total to follow. For a translator, this matters because the words certainty and flexibility usually attach to the instrument rather than to the outcome, and a document that promises one is promising something the other cannot deliver.

questions.explanation: A tax offers price certainty, a cap quantity certainty and a standard neither, so the instrument determines where certainty sits. Rendering them interchangeably changes what a document promises.
questions.hint: Ask where each scheme places its certainty.

It also leaves open how much of the burden reaches households through prices, how the revenue is used, and how the domestic price compares with prices abroad. Translators should resist rendering a price as a quota, a target or a guarantee of a particular outcome.

questions.explanation: A price shifts incentives and leaves quantity, incidence and revenue use open. Rendering it as a quota or a guarantee changes a flexible instrument into a rigid commitment in the target language.
questions.hint: Separate what is fixed from what is left open.
